title: How to start over?
summary: Conversion is not self-improvement, but a change of direction: repentance and the surrender of your life to God, in which he gives you new birth, a new heart, and makes you a new creation. It is the beginning of a relationship renewed every day, not a one-time act to be checked off.

items.comment: The first words of Jesus' public mission: "repent and believe in the Gospel." Repentance and faith are two sides of the same turn toward God.

questions.text: What does "to repent" mean - merely improving behavior, or changing whom I trust and toward whom I am headed?

items.label: "repentance" is a change of mind and direction
items.content: The Greek *metanoia* does not primarily mean "sorrow" or "punishment," but a "change of mind and attitude" leading to a change in the direction of life. It is not self-flagellation, but a new way of seeing from which a new path follows. Repentance and faith in Mark 1:15 are two sides of one turn: I turn away from my former path because I have come to trust the Good News.

questions.text: How does understanding conversion as a "change of mind and direction" (rather than mere regret) change the practice of repentance?

items.comment: "Repent and turn back, so that your sins may be wiped out." Repentance is not a punishment I impose on myself - it is the road to freedom and "refreshing."

questions.text: What has "repentance" been associated with for you so far - a burden or relief? What does this text change?

items.comment: The prodigal son first "came to himself," and then "got up and went to his father." Conversion is awareness plus a real movement toward home.

questions.text: Which part tends to be harder: seeing the truth about yourself, or taking the first step back? Why?

items.label: restored to sonship, not on probation (Luke 15)
items.content: The son hoped at best for the status of a hired hand, but the father restores him fully as a son: a robe (dignity), a ring (authority and belonging to the family), sandals (worn by free men, not slaves), and a feast. This is a picture of conversion in God's eyes: not a "trial period" or a "second tier," but immediate, full restoration into the family. Returning to God does not make us servants on conditions - it makes us children again.

items.comment: Paul distinguishes "godly sorrow," which "produces repentance," from the barren sorrow "of this world." The point is regret that leads to change, not self-flagellation.

questions.text: How does the sorrow that leads to God and to change differ from the sorrow that only drags you down?

items.comment: "Let the wicked forsake his way... and return to the Lord, and he will have mercy." Conversion is forsaking one road and receiving God's forgiveness, which is "abundant."

questions.text: What does it say about God that the one who returns is met not with reproach, but with "abundant" forgiveness?

items.label: the Hebrew "shuv": turn around and return
items.content: The Old Testament equivalent of conversion is *shuv* - "to turn back, to turn around and return." It is a word from the language of the road: someone was walking in one direction, stops, turns around, and returns home. That is why the prophets cry out "return (come back) to the Lord." Conversion is therefore a turning of the whole person toward God, not merely a feeling of regret or a cosmetic improvement of deeds.

items.comment: The response to God's mercy is to offer "yourselves" as a "living sacrifice." Not a fragment of life or a Sunday - the whole of it.

questions.text: What is hardest for you to give to God "as a whole," and what would you gladly keep just for yourself?

items.comment: "It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me." Surrendering your life is not the loss of self but an exchange: my old "I" for the life of Christ in me.

questions.text: Does surrendering your life to God sound more like a loss or a gain to you? Which wins out?

items.comment: Jesus invites us to take up the cross "daily" and follow him. The word "daily" shows that surrendering your life is a rhythm, not a one-time decision.

questions.text: What might "daily" following Jesus mean for you - in the concrete details of tomorrow?

items.comment: Jesus tells Nicodemus: "unless one is born again, he cannot see the Kingdom of God." A new beginning is needed, not a touch-up of the old life.

questions.text: Why does Jesus speak of "new birth" rather than simply "improvement"? What does that suggest about our situation?

items.label: "again" also means "from above" (John 3:3)
items.content: The Greek *anothen* has a double meaning: "again" and "from above, from God." This ambiguity is deliberate: new birth is at once a new beginning and a work that comes from above (from the Spirit). Nicodemus' misunderstanding (he took it only as "a second time," in human terms) highlights the point: the source of this birth is heaven, not human biology or human will alone.

questions.text: What do we gain by reading new birth as both "again" and "from above"? What do we lose by taking only one meaning?

items.comment: Birth "of the Spirit" is the work of God, not our achievement: "what is born of the Spirit is spirit." We are born - but Someone else gives us birth.

questions.text: What does it mean that new life cannot be "produced" by effort, but can only be received?

items.comment: Jesus compares the Spirit's working to the wind: we do not control it, but we see its effects. New birth can be mysterious, yet real and recognizable.

questions.text: By what "effects" (as by the sound of the wind) can you recognize that God's Spirit is at work in someone's life?

items.comment: "Born again... of imperishable seed, through the word of God." The instrument of new birth is the living Word - which is why feeding on the Bible is so important.

questions.text: What role can regular meeting with God's Word play in being "born again"?

items.label: "regeneration" / palingenesis (Titus 3:5)
items.content: New birth is also called *palingenesia* - "coming into being again, regeneration" (Titus 3:5: "the washing of regeneration"). Jesus uses the same word for the renewal of the whole world at the end (Matt 19:28). This is a striking pairing: the same power that will one day renew the entire universe is already at work in the person being regenerated. Conversion is the beginning of a new creation that will be completed on a cosmic scale.

sections.heading: A new heart and a new creation

items.comment: God promises: "I will give you a new heart... I will remove the heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh." Transformation begins from within, where we ourselves cannot bring about change.

questions.text: What does a "heart of stone" need in order to become a "heart of flesh" - and who is the one bringing about that change?

items.label: the new heart as a promise of the New Covenant
items.content: Ezek 36:26-27 belongs to the promises of the New Covenant (cf. Jer 31:31-34), given to the people in exile, when their own strength had failed. God announces not only forgiveness, but inner transformation: the Law written on the heart and his own Spirit enabling obedience. This is the biblical foundation for the claim that obedience is the fruit of God's working in a person (a transformed heart), and not a preliminary condition that a person must meet on their own.

questions.text: How does the promise of a "new heart" explain why real change begins with God, and not with gritting your teeth?

items.comment: "I will put my Spirit within you and cause you to walk according to... my statutes." Even obedience is a gift: it is God who "causes" us to want and to be able.

questions.text: How does it change the picture of a godly life that God not only commands but himself enables it from within?

items.comment: "If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation; the old has passed away, the new has come." The believer's identity is defined not by the past, but by the new beginning in Christ.

questions.text: What would it mean for you to see yourself not through the lens of the "old," but of the "new creation"?

items.label: "new creation" (2 Cor 5:17)
items.content: Paul uses the phrase *kaine ktisis* - "new creation." The same word (*ktisis*) is used by the Bible to describe the act of creating the world. The message is powerful: when someone is in Christ, something happens of the same magnitude as "in the beginning" - God creates anew. The believer's identity is therefore not an "improved version of the old," but a new work of the Creator.

items.comment: The image of changing clothes: "to put off the old self... and put on the new self, created after God." New life has a real, noticeable shape.

questions.text: What in your life would be worth "taking off," and what "putting on," if this were a picture of a new wardrobe?

items.comment: "God works in you both to will and to act." New life is a cooperation in which the initiative and the power belong to God, and the response - to me.

questions.text: How do you understand the balance: God "works the willing and the acting," while I am to yield to him, not replace him with my own effort?

items.label: cooperation, not competition (Phil 2:12-13)
items.content: Paul places side by side two things that seem contradictory: "work out your own salvation with fear" and immediately "it is God who works in you both to will and to act." They are not in opposition: my effort does not replace God or force him - it is the response to his prior working in me. New life is not a race of "me versus God," but a cooperation in which his power is first and last, and I do not block it but yield to it.

sections.heading: A daily relationship, not a one-time act

items.comment: "Our inner self is being renewed day by day." New life is not a single event in the past, but a daily renewal.

questions.text: What might "being renewed" with God practically mean in your day - in the morning, during the day, in the evening?

items.comment: When I fall, the way back is open: "if we confess our sins, he... will forgive." Conversion is also a daily returning, not a one-time start with no room for stumbling.

questions.text: What gives the assurance that a stumble does not cancel the relationship, but that you can immediately return to God after it?

items.comment: Paul "forgets what lies behind" and "strains toward what lies ahead." New life has direction and a goal - it is a road, not a finish line crossed once for all.

questions.text: What from the past is hardest for you to "leave behind" so that you can keep following Jesus?

application.text: Conversion is not heroic self-improvement, but a turn: I turn away from my own road and return to God, surrendering my life to him. And then he does what I cannot - he gives me new birth, gives me a new heart, makes me a new creation. This is not a one-time act to check off in the calendar, but the beginning of a relationship renewed every day, in which even after a fall the way back is always open.
application.challenge: Set aside this week one specific moment of the day (e.g. the morning) for "renewing" the relationship: give God the coming day and one matter in which you want him to "work the willing and the acting" (Phil 2:13). If you stumble, do not postpone returning - turn at once to 1 John 1:9. At the end of the week, write down one "fruit" you have noticed (like the sound of the wind from John 3:8) by which you recognize that it is not only your effort, but the working of the Spirit.
